questions.question: What is a Git branch and how is it implemented internally?
questions.title: What Is a Git Branch?
questions.direct_answer: A Git branch is a lightweight movable pointer to a specific commit — creating a branch is just creating a file containing a 40-character commit hash, which is why it's nearly instantaneous.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Git branches work at a conceptual level, not just the commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking branches are copies of the codebase — they're just pointers, not copies
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the HEAD pointer and how it tracks your current branch

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A Git branch is, at its core, just a lightweight pointer to a commit. Literally, under the hood, a branch is a file in .git/refs/heads/ that contains the 40-character SHA-1 hash of the commit it points to. That's it. There's no copying of files, no forking of the codebase. When you make a new commit on a branch, Git updates that pointer to point to the new commit. This is why creating a branch in Git is essentially instantaneous and uses almost no disk space — compare that to SVN where a branch means copying an entire directory tree. There's also a special pointer called HEAD, which tells Git which branch you currently have checked out. When you run 'git checkout mybranch', HEAD starts pointing to mybranch. This pointer model is what makes Git's branching model so powerful — you can have dozens of branches representing different features or experiments, and switching between them is just updating a file.

sections.title: Key Points
content: A branch is a lightweight pointer (file with a commit SHA) — not a copy of the codebase
Creating a branch is nearly instant and uses minimal disk space
HEAD is a special pointer that indicates the currently checked-out branch
When you commit on a branch, the branch pointer automatically advances to the new commit
This design enables Git's feature-branch workflow: cheap to create, cheap to delete

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: A Git branch isn't a copy of your code — it's literally just a tiny text file with a commit hash in it.

beats.content: A Git branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. Internally it's just a file in .git/refs/heads/ containing a 40-character SHA hash. No code is copied — the branch simply knows which commit it's currently pointing at.

Branches let you isolate work. You create a branch for a new feature, commit freely there, and the main branch stays untouched until you're ready to merge. Because they're just pointers, creating or deleting branches costs almost nothing.

content: Branch pointer: a file with a commit SHA that auto-advances every time you make a new commit
HEAD: a special pointer telling Git which branch you're currently on
Detached HEAD: HEAD points to a raw commit hash instead of a branch name

beats.content: When you create feature/add-login in your Spring Boot project, Git just writes one file — .git/refs/heads/feature/add-login — containing the current commit hash. candidates miss: switching branches is also just updating that HEAD file, which is why git switch is instant no matter how large the project is.

content: Thinking a branch copies all your files — it doesn't, which is why you can have 20 branches with zero extra storage
Confusing HEAD with origin — HEAD is always local and tells Git where your next commit goes

speakable_v2.cap: Branches are just pointers — cheap, fast, and the foundation of every team Git workflow.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git checkout -b' and 'git switch -c' for creating branches?
questions.title: git checkout -b vs git switch -c
questions.direct_answer: Both create and switch to a new branch, but 'git switch -c' is the modern, purpose-built command for branch operations introduced in Git 2.23, while 'git checkout' is the older overloaded command that also handles file restoration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern Git commands and understanding of why the split happened
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing 'git switch' exists — being stuck on checkout-only knowledge
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 'git restore' was also introduced alongside 'git switch' to take over file-restoration from checkout

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Both commands achieve the same result — they create a new branch and switch to it — but they come from different eras of Git. 'git checkout -b branchname' is the classic command, and it works fine. The problem with 'git checkout' is that it's heavily overloaded — it's used for switching branches, checking out specific files, detaching HEAD, and more. That made it confusing for beginners. In Git 2.23, the team split the responsibilities. 'git switch' is now dedicated purely to branch-related operations: 'git switch branchname' to switch, 'git switch -c newbranch' to create and switch. Similarly, 'git restore' was introduced to handle file-level operations that were previously done with 'git checkout -- filename'. Both 'git switch' and 'git restore' are safer because they have clearer, more predictable behavior. Most modern tutorials use 'git switch', but you'll still see 'git checkout -b' everywhere in older docs, Stack Overflow answers, and scripts — so knowing both is important.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'git checkout -b branch': classic way to create + switch; still widely used
'git switch -c branch': modern equivalent, introduced in Git 2.23, branch-specific
git checkout was split because it was too overloaded (branches + files + detached HEAD)
'git restore' handles file restoration (the other half of what checkout did)
Both commands are valid — know both for reading older docs and scripts

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: Both do the same thing — but one of them is trying to do way too much, which is exactly why the newer one was invented.

content: git checkout -b branchname is the classic command from Git's early days. It creates a new branch and switches to it in one step. It still works perfectly, but git checkout is overloaded — it also restores files, detaches HEAD, and handles tags. That overlap caused a lot of beginner confusion.

git switch -c branchname is the modern replacement introduced in Git 2.23. It's dedicated purely to branch operations. git switch branchname to switch, git switch -c branchname to create and switch. Cleaner and harder to misuse.
Use git switch -c in new projects and modern tutorials — it's clearer and purpose-built for branches
Know git checkout -b too — you'll see it in older Stack Overflow answers, CI scripts, and legacy docs

beats.content: Starting a feature in your Spring Boot project: git switch -c feature/add-login creates the branch and puts you on it. Same result as git checkout -b feature/add-login — pick whichever the team prefers.

speakable_v2.cap: Prefer git switch -c in new work, but recognize git checkout -b everywhere — they produce identical results.

questions.question: What is a feature branch workflow and why is it used?
questions.title: Feature Branch Workflow
questions.direct_answer: The feature branch workflow means each new feature or bug fix is developed on its own dedicated branch off main, keeping the main branch stable and enabling parallel development and code review via pull requests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of team-based Git workflows — this is the daily reality for most developers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing directly to main in a team setting — this is a major antipattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that feature branches enable parallel development — two developers can work on two features without interfering with each other

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The feature branch workflow is the standard way most teams use Git. The idea is simple: the 'main' branch always contains stable, production-ready code. Nobody commits directly to main. Whenever you start working on a new feature or bug fix, you create a dedicated branch: 'git switch -c feature/user-authentication'. All your commits for that feature go on that branch. When you're done, you open a pull request to merge that branch into main. This workflow has several big advantages. First, main stays clean and deployable at all times. Second, it enables parallel development — you and a colleague can both work on separate features simultaneously on their own branches without stepping on each other. Third, it gates code into main through a review process — the pull request is where the team reviews your code, catches bugs, and ensures quality before it merges. The branch is typically deleted after it merges to keep the repository tidy.

sections.title: Key Points
content: One branch per feature/bugfix; main branch always stays stable and deployable
Branch naming: feature/add-login, fix/null-pointer-bug, chore/update-dependencies
Enables parallel development — multiple developers work on separate branches simultaneously
Code review happens via pull request before merging into main
Delete the branch after merge to keep the repo clean ('git branch -d branchname')

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: Committing directly to main is the number-one antipattern freshers bring to their first team job — here's the right way.

beats.content: The feature branch workflow means you never commit directly to main. Instead, every new feature or bug fix gets its own dedicated branch off main. All your commits go there, and when you're done you open a pull request to review and merge it back.

Main needs to stay stable and deployable at all times. If everyone commits directly to main, one broken commit can block the entire team. Branches isolate work and let the team verify quality through pull request review before anything reaches main.

content: main: always stable, always deployable — never commit here directly
feature branch: isolated workspace for one feature or fix — git switch -c feature/add-login
pull request: the review gate — code is inspected and approved before merging into main

beats.content: Two devs on your Spring Boot team both create branches: feature/add-login and feature/payment-gateway. They work in parallel without touching each other's code. production trap: if they both committed directly to main, one merge would constantly break the other's work — feature branches prevent exactly that.

content: Committing directly to main in a shared repo is a serious antipattern — most teams protect main with branch rules
Long-lived branches drift from main and produce huge merge conflicts — aim to merge within days, not weeks

questions.question: How do you list, create, and delete branches in Git?
questions.title: Managing Git Branches: List, Create, Delete
questions.direct_answer: Use 'git branch' to list local branches, 'git branch -a' to include remote branches, 'git branch branchname' or 'git switch -c branchname' to create, and 'git branch -d branchname' to delete a merged branch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical command knowledge for everyday Git operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using -D (force delete) instead of -d (safe delete) without understanding the difference
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that '-d' is safe (refuses to delete unmerged branches) while '-D' force-deletes regardless

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: For day-to-day branch management, you need a handful of commands. To list branches: 'git branch' shows all local branches with an asterisk next to the current one. 'git branch -a' shows local and remote tracking branches. 'git branch -r' shows only remote branches. To create a branch without switching: 'git branch branchname'. To create and switch: 'git switch -c branchname' or the older 'git checkout -b branchname'. To switch to an existing branch: 'git switch branchname'. To delete: 'git branch -d branchname' is the safe version — it will refuse to delete the branch if it has unmerged commits, protecting you from accidentally losing work. 'git branch -D branchname' is the force delete — use it when you're sure you want to delete an unmerged branch, like abandoning a feature. To delete a remote branch you use 'git push origin --delete branchname' — that's a push command, not a branch command, which trips people up.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'git branch': list local branches; 'git branch -a': list all including remote
'git switch -c name' or 'git checkout -b name': create and switch to new branch
'git branch -d name': safe delete (won't delete unmerged branches)
'git branch -D name': force delete (deletes regardless of merge status)
'git push origin --delete name': delete a branch on the remote

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: There's a crucial difference between -d and -D for deleting branches — one protects you, the other doesn't.

beats.content: Git gives you a small set of commands to manage branches day-to-day: listing what exists, creating new ones, switching between them, and cleaning up finished branches. Knowing when to use the safe vs force variants of delete is especially important.

Branch management commands exist so you can navigate a multi-branch workflow fluidly. Without them you'd be stuck on one line of development — with them you can juggle features, fixes, and experiments cleanly.

content: git branch: list local branches; git branch -a includes remote tracking refs
git switch -c branchname: create and switch in one step (modern); git checkout -b still works
git branch -d: safe delete — refuses to delete if branch has unmerged commits
git branch -D: force delete — removes regardless of merge status, use carefully
git push origin --delete branchname: removes the branch from the remote server

beats.content: After merging feature/add-login into main via a pull request, run git branch -d feature/add-login. sharp edge: if you accidentally run git branch -D on a branch with 3 days of unmerged work, those commits become unreachable — -d is the safe guard that prevents that mistake.

content: Deleting a remote branch requires git push origin --delete — not git branch -d which only affects local
Using -D habitually instead of -d removes your safety net for accidental deletions

speakable_v2.cap: Use -d for safe cleanup after merging, and -D only when you're sure you want to discard unmerged work.

questions.question: What is the HEAD pointer in Git?
questions.title: The HEAD Pointer in Git
questions.direct_answer: HEAD is a special Git pointer that tells you which branch (or commit) you currently have checked out — it's essentially 'where you are now' in the repository.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's internal model — HEAD is referenced in many error messages and commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing HEAD with the remote — HEAD is always local
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain detached HEAD state and when it occurs (checking out a specific commit hash)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HEAD is Git's way of knowing where you currently are in the repository. Normally HEAD points to a branch name — for example, HEAD → main. When you commit, the branch pointer advances and HEAD moves with it. When you run 'git checkout somebranch', HEAD starts pointing to that branch instead. HEAD is how Git knows which branch to advance when you make a new commit. There's a special state called 'detached HEAD' — this happens when you check out a specific commit hash directly, rather than a branch name: 'git checkout abc1234'. In this state, HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch. You can look around and even make commits, but those commits won't belong to any branch — if you switch away without creating a branch, those commits become unreachable and will eventually be garbage collected. The fix is simple: if you're in detached HEAD state and want to keep your commits, run 'git switch -c new-branch-name' to create a branch at that point.

sections.title: Key Points
content: HEAD points to the currently checked-out branch (normally) or commit (detached HEAD)
When you commit, the current branch pointer and HEAD both advance to the new commit
Detached HEAD: happens when you checkout a specific commit hash, not a branch name
In detached HEAD, commits are not attached to any branch and can be lost
Fix detached HEAD with: 'git switch -c new-branch-name' to anchor your commits

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: HEAD sounds scary, but it's just Git's way of saying 'you are here' — until it gets detached, which is where things get interesting.

beats.content: HEAD is a special pointer in Git that always tells you where you currently are. Normally it points to a branch name — HEAD → main. When you make a commit, the branch advances and HEAD follows it automatically.

Git needs to know which branch to advance when you commit. HEAD is the mechanism. It also lets Git know where to rebase or cherry-pick relative to 'now', which is why you see it so often in advanced commands.

content: Normal HEAD: points to a branch name — commits advance that branch forward
Detached HEAD: points directly to a commit hash — you're not on any branch
HEAD~1: shorthand for the commit one step before HEAD; HEAD~2 is two steps back

beats.content: In a Spring Boot project you run git checkout a3f9bc2 to look at an old version. Git prints 'You are in detached HEAD state.' production trap: if you make commits here and then switch away without saving a branch, those commits become unreachable garbage. Run git switch -c hotfix/temp to anchor them immediately.

content: Confusing HEAD with origin/HEAD — HEAD is always local, tracking where your working copy is
Making commits in detached HEAD state and forgetting to create a branch — those commits will be lost

speakable_v2.cap: HEAD is your 'you are here' marker — keep it on a branch and you'll never lose commits.
